extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers; students of history, literary criticism, and philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging historical actors (e.g., judges) and philosophical systems, as used in a biographical/critical essay on Bacon; focuses on evidence, publicity/legal sanction, moral character under temptation, and the value of philosophy measured by utility and progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence does not imply innocence
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that practices (theft, cheating, perjury, adultery, gift-taking by judges) were common in an age does not prove they were considered innocent or justifiable by contemporaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate frequency with moral acceptance; examine laws and public opinion. The essay cites Hugh Latimer's sermons as evidence that corrupt practices were widely condemned even when common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneous legal and parliamentary action as evidence of moral standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosecution, trial, conviction, and sentencing of a person by contemporaries is the best evidence of what that age considered criminal or culpable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the House of Commons and House of Lords prosecuted and punished an individual, this demonstrates that his own age regarded the conduct as blameworthy — one should not relativize away contemporary judgment without strong contrary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity and legal sanction distinguish perquisites from bribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Payments that are legally sanctioned, made publicly, and have amounts regulated by law (perquisites/fees) differ fundamentally from private presents negotiated between suitor and magistrate (bribes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a payment was corrupt, check: Was there a legal right to the fee? Was it regulated by law? Was it given publicly or secretly? The French example (legal fees) is contrasted with Bacon's privately bargained presents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy of receipt implies corrupt intent
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person accepts presents secretly in some cases but only publicly in one exceptional case, the secrecy of the other instances suggests knowledge that those receipts were improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use patterns of publicity: a solitary public present (especially when non-judicial and amicable) combined with other secret presents supports inference of guilt; public acceptance during non-judicial, consensual matters is less culpable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of high-ranking agents does not excuse corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing bishops, privy counsellors, members of Parliament, or other persons of rank as intermediaries does not prove that payments were not corrupt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept appeals to the social rank of participants as evidence of probity; historical examples show high people engaged in low actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern-detection via dissatisfied suitors reveals systemic corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive systems of corruption are often exposed when a suitor who has paid but not received the expected favor becomes an accuser; those who benefited remain silent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When investigating alleged corruption, pay attention to complainants who paid and lost (they have incentive to speak); examples: the Goezman/Beaumarchais case — bribery would have remained hidden had the briber won.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context matters for judging a gift's impropriety (judicial vs amicable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A present received in the course of an amicable, non-judicial arbitration (both parties satisfied) is less likely to be corrupt than gifts received in secret in matters where the receiver sat judicially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate whether the recipient was acting judicially or simply facilitating a private settlement; publicity and mutual consent reduce the appearance of corruption, but do not automatically absolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and evidentiary weight of confession and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Confession, mitigation, and the tone of the proceeding (decency, gravity, moderated justice) affect judgments about culpability; a temperate prosecution and mitigation after sentence are relevant to assessing fairness but not to innocence if evidence is strong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both the process (fairness, lack of personal animosity) and the substance (evidence of wrongdoing); the essay argues Bacon's conviction reflected irresistible evidence despite humane treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical value: utility (fruit) as primary criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A sound philosophy should aim at 'fruit' — the multiplying of human enjoyments and mitigating human sufferings; utility (practical benefit) is a central measure of philosophical merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate philosophies by their capacity to relieve human ills, produce inventions, practical improvements, and to serve 'commodis humanis inservire' (in the service of human comforts). Bacon's programme is offered as exemplar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical value: progress and accumulation of useful truth
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable philosophy is progressive — it enables accumulation of useful truths across generations (a heritage of truth), rather than perpetual disputation with no net gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge systems by whether they produce cumulative knowledge and practical advances rather than being a recurrent treadmill of argument. The absence of accumulation (no harvest after much ploughing) is a sign of failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting sterile disputation as a standard of failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophies that end in controversy, fine dialectic, or moral perfection-as-abstract-theory, without producing practical improvements, are to be criticized as unfruitful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of admiring intellectual display when it generates little real-world benefit; compare the 'treadmill' of ancient philosophy to Bacon's insistence on useful outcomes (e.g., technologies, bettering life).

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosopher's character: humility and attention to humble improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine philosophic spirit includes 'majestic humility' and a willingness to pursue even lowly practical inventions and improvements for human benefit (Bacon's 'architectus... operarius... bajulus').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess philosophers by whether they embrace practical, sometimes humble, tasks to improve life (e.g., inventions, mechanical improvements), instead of scorning usefulness as beneath dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness judged by tangible inventions and improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: One way to test the value of a philosophy or age is the extent to which it produces tangible improvements (eg., the arch, use of metals, printing, gunpowder) that benefit human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count concrete technological or institutional advances as evidence of fruitful thought; philosophical systems that neglect this are criticized for contented despondency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral assessment requires examining conduct under temptation
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge a person's moral character, consider how they act when exposed to strong temptation and opportunity for gain (trustworthiness under pressure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A life spent in literary retirement might conceal weaknesses revealed by public office and strong temptation; excellence in study does not guarantee probity in practice.
